Checked each Section 26 criterion against its requirement. FR-5, FR-8, NFR-1, NFR-2, NFR-4 and NFR-6 either cannot demonstrate their requirement as written or would fail against the design. FR-10, FR-12 and NFR-9 are adequate.

A Redis key made only of the client key, served with no merchant or hash check, makes keys like order numbers collide across 15,000 merchants and returns another merchant's stored response. That breaks P3, FR-5 (including the 422 rule) and tenant isolation.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 9.2 and the Section 24 idempotency row, change the key to idem:resp:{merchant_id}:{sha256(idempotency_key)}. Store request_hash with the cached response and check it on every hit, returning 422 on a mismatch. Add FR-5 acceptance cases where two merchants use the same key and where a reused key is sent with a different body after the first request completed.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Keeps FR-5 and P3 intact, stops responses leaking between merchants, and prevents missed charges for colliding merchants.
recommendation.issue: The fast-path key leaves out merchant_id, and the fast path skips request-hash validation.
recommendation.rationale: P3 and FR-5 scope idempotency to the (merchant, key) pair. The DynamoDB path does this correctly, but the fast path that sits in front of it does not.
recommendation.verification: FR-5 contract test: merchants A and B send the same Idempotency-Key and get separate payments. A reused key with a changed body returns 422 whether the response comes from Redis or DynamoDB.

findings.statement: Section 9.2 stores and looks up the fast-path response under idem:resp:{idempotency_key} and returns it without reaching DynamoDB. That key does not include the merchant, so it contradicts P3 and FR-5. Section 9.1 says merchants often use order or invoice numbers as keys, so two merchants sending the same key is likely. When that happens, merchant B gets merchant A's payment object (a data leak) and no payment is created for B, who may still ship the goods. Because the fast path also never compares the request hash, the HTTP 422 rule in FR-5 is not enforced for any reused key that has completed.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path is not scoped by merchant and skips the body-hash check

If about 3.8% of card payments cascade, the slowest 1% are mostly cascaded payments. Any of those triggered by the 2,500 ms timeout already exceed 1,500 ms, so the p99 in Section 21.1 cannot leave cascades out and NFR-2 is likely to fail its own test.

next_step.action: Measure the timeout share of retryable outcomes from 2025 data and choose the timeout or requirement change before Phase 4.

recommendation.change_summary: Rewrite the Section 21.1 cascade paragraph using the 3.8% retryable rate. Then choose one: (a) cut the per-attempt timeout and set a total cascade deadline that fits within 1,500 ms; (b) cascade only on fast-fail outcomes (5xx, connection refused, soft declines) and not on timeouts; or (c) restate NFR-2 as a separate p99 for non-cascaded and cascaded payments. Model the cascade tail separately in the budget.
recommendation.expected_benefit: A latency budget that holds together and an NFR-2 that can actually be achieved and verified.
recommendation.issue: The latency budget's cascade-share figure contradicts the baseline, and the cascade timeout is longer than the whole NFR-2 budget.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-2 explicitly includes cascades, and the acceptance test injects 3.8% retryable outcomes.
recommendation.verification: NFR-2 benchmark with 3.8% retryable injection that includes the timeout share, reporting p99 for all payments and for cascaded payments separately.

findings.statement: Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 because 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade'. Section 10.5 gives 3.8% retryable outcomes, cascading recovers about 31% of them, and the NFR-2 acceptance test injects 3.8% retryable outcomes. With about 3.8% of payments cascading, the cascade path falls inside the 99th percentile. A timeout-triggered cascade alone takes at least 2,500 ms plus a second round trip, well over the 1,500 ms in NFR-2. As specified, NFR-2 (which explicitly includes 'any cascade') is likely to fail its own acceptance test.
findings.title: Latency budget excludes cascades using a 1% figure that contradicts the 3.8% retryable baseline

Async replication with sub-second lag gives an RPO above zero, not zero. The payment table has no idempotency_key or request_hash column, so it cannot be used to rebuild idempotency records. A 30-minute RTO exceeds the 0.05% of a 30-day month (about 21.6 minutes) that NFR-3 allows.

next_step.owner: Platform architecture lead with Finance and Risk owners

recommendation.change_summary: Pick one: (a) restate NFR-4 as a non-zero RPO (for example ≤1 s) with a documented post-failover reconciliation of lost-window payments against acquirer records; or (b) add a synchronous cross-region commit for authorisations and postings and include its latency cost in Section 21. Add idempotency_key and request_hash to the payment table (unique on merchant, key), or replicate the idempotency table across regions. State whether a regional failover counts against NFR-3, or reconcile the 30-minute RTO with the 99.95% target.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Achievable, consistent RPO, RTO and availability targets, and no duplicate charges after failover (FR-5).
recommendation.issue: NFR-4's zero RPO and NFR-3's availability target cannot be met by the Section 20 design, and the idempotency rebuild has no data to work from.
recommendation.rationale: Either the requirement or the mechanism has to change before the NFR-4 game day can pass.
recommendation.verification: NFR-4 game day with writes in flight at failure: measure lost postings against the restated RPO, and replay in-flight requests to confirm there are no duplicate authorisations.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorised payments and ledger postings when a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 replicates Aurora asynchronously with lag under a second, so a sudden region loss can lose committed postings. Section 20.2 also rebuilds in-flight idempotency state 'from the payment table', but the Section 19 payment table has no idempotency key or request hash, so duplicate provider calls are possible after failover. Separately, a 30-minute failover is longer than the roughly 21.9 minutes of monthly downtime that NFR-3's 99.95% allows. The NFR-4 game day (unplanned failover, every posting present) would fail as designed.
findings.title: Zero-RPO and availability targets contradict async replication, the 30-minute RTO and the data model

A timeout does not mean the issuer declined. Discarding a late approval while a cascade succeeds elsewhere leaves a second live authorisation for the same payment with no void, which contradicts FR-5 and P1.

recommendation.change_summary: In Section 11.2, mark a timed-out attempt as UNKNOWN rather than discarded. On a late approval, or through a status query by the Section 20.3 sweeper, send an authorisation reversal to that acquirer and record it on the attempt. Alternatively, send the reversal immediately on timeout before cascading. Remove the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' claim. Add a late-approval case to the FR-7 cascade simulation.
recommendation.expected_benefit: No orphaned customer holds and FR-5 holds in the timeout case.
recommendation.issue: Timed-out attempts that are later approved are never reversed.
recommendation.rationale: FR-5 limits each request to one downstream authorisation, and P1 needs every provider outcome to be reflected in the payment record.
recommendation.verification: Simulator injects an approval at 3,000 ms on attempt 1 while attempt 2 is approved. The test asserts a reversal is sent for attempt 1 and only one live authorisation remains.

findings.statement: Section 11.2 discards responses that arrive after the 2,500 ms timeout and says cascading 'cannot create a duplicate charge' because the ledger records only the approved attempt. When an issuer approves the timed-out attempt and the next acquirer approves the cascade, the customer has two authorisation holds and one of them is never released. The design has no step to reverse or void it, which breaks FR-5's 'at most one authorization' and P1, and the ledger-only argument does not cover this case. The FR-7 acceptance test does not inject late approvals.
findings.title: No reversal path for late approvals on timed-out cascade attempts

Model settlement separately from refund state, either as a settlement_status attribute or by allowing PARTIALLY_REFUNDED/REFUNDED -> SETTLED. Define how REVIEW holds are represented (a capture_hold flag or an AUTHORISED_ON_HOLD state) and what REVIEW does for wallets, which have no capture. Define multiple partial captures (CAPTURED -> CAPTURED with captured_minor ≤ amount_minor). Build the FR-2 property test from end-to-end flow scenarios as well as from the Section 7.2 graph.
recommendation.expected_benefit: FR-2 can be met in practice, and reconciliation of refunded payments matches automatically, which supports NFR-8.
recommendation.issue: Section 7.2 is incomplete compared with the flows in Sections 8, 11.4 and 16.2.
recommendation.rationale: FR-2 makes Section 7.2 the full set of allowed transitions, and Section 27 rates it Ready.

findings.statement: FR-2 allows only the transitions in Section 7.2, but several flows elsewhere need ones that are missing. Section 11.4 returns FAILED for a wallet or bank payment sitting in REQUIRES_ACTION, and a failed 3DS challenge needs the same, but REQUIRES_ACTION can only go to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED. Section 16.2 moves matched payments to SETTLED, but a payment refunded before settlement (PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED) cannot reach SETTLED, which would create reconciliation exceptions and put NFR-8's 99.9% auto-match at risk. The REVIEW 'authorize-and-hold-capture' outcome and repeated partial captures have no state representation either. The FR-2 property test checks conformance to Section 7.2, so it cannot detect these gaps.
findings.title: State machine lacks transitions that other sections depend on

55% of 2,000 TPS is 1,100 card TPS, below the 1,500 TPS trigger, so there is one HSM through 2027. Losing it fails every card authorisation, cascades included, for the whole restore time, which conflicts with Section 20.1 and NFR-3.

Add the Vault store, the CloudHSM cluster (backup copy or pre-provisioned cluster) and the CDE EKS cluster in ap-southeast-3 to Section 20.2, with a target time. findings.statement: Section 12.3 keeps all KEKs on one HSM in ap-southeast-1a and adds a second only above 1,500 sustained card TPS. Card volume at the 2027 peak is about 55% of 2,000, or 1,100 TPS, so the second HSM would never be added at design volume. If the HSM is lost, every detokenise returns 503, which is treated as retryable, and every cascade also needs detokenise, so all card authorisations fail until a new HSM is restored from backup. This contradicts Section 20.1 ('every service ... three AZs') and puts NFR-3 at risk. Section 20.2 also says nothing about Vault or CloudHSM recovery in ap-southeast-3, so NFR-4 does not cover cards.
findings.title: CDE has a single HSM in one AZ and no DR path, which conflicts with the three-AZ and availability requirements

findings.statement: Section 24 confirms network tokens as the main card-on-file credential from launch. Section 27 rates the Vault Ready, and Section 28 marks Phase 3 (card-on-file with network tokens) 'No - ready'. Backlog item 2, however, says the VTS/MDES token-requestor registration and the commercial agreement have not been applied for. FR-14 and the Phase 3 dependency therefore rest on an open item with an unknown lead time. The backlog acknowledges the item; this finding points out that the readiness and phase tables do not reflect it.
findings.title: Network tokens 'from launch' depend on a token-requestor application not yet submitted

A sequential replay test cannot show concurrent deduplication. A sweeper that starts from payments cannot find idempotency locks taken before any payment existed.

next_step.action: Add the concurrent, cross-merchant and crash-injection cases to the FR-5 test design.

recommendation.change_summary: Extend the FR-5 test in Section 26.1: N parallel identical requests give exactly one simulator authorisation, one 201 and the others 409 or an identical replay; two merchants send the same key; a pod is killed between lock and payment creation, and between authorisation and completion. In Sections 9.2 and 20.3, add a sweep of DynamoDB IN_PROGRESS records older than a threshold with no payment_id, releasing them or marking them failed.
recommendation.expected_benefit: FR-5 is demonstrated under the conditions that matter, and keys cannot be locked out for 24 hours.
recommendation.issue: The FR-5 criterion does not cover the concurrency it is meant to verify, and lock recovery has a hole.
recommendation.rationale: Concurrent duplicates during retry storms are the main risk FR-5 addresses.
recommendation.verification: Extended FR-5 test suite passes in CI and in the Phase 9 chaos runs.

findings.statement: FR-5 requires the same response and at most one provider call 'including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently'. The acceptance test only resends after the first response has arrived, so it never exercises the conditional-put lock, the 409 path, the Redis fast path across merchants, or crash recovery. There is also a missing error path: the sweeper scans payments in AUTHORISING, so a pod that crashes after the DynamoDB put but before the payment row is created leaves an IN_PROGRESS record with no payment to resolve. That key then returns 409 until the 24-hour TTL expires.
findings.title: FR-5 acceptance test omits concurrency, cross-merchant and crash cases

The 1,800 WCU figure assumes small items and no index write cost, and the per-partition ceiling is unsourced. A uniform load test would not reveal throttling on M-0001's partition key.

next_step.action: Confirm the DynamoDB partition limits and run a single-key benchmark at 900 TPS with production-sized items.

recommendation.change_summary: Check the per-partition write limit and item-size WCU rules for DynamoDB, including LSI effects. Recompute Section 9.3 with real item sizes. If the margin is thin, consider a partition key that spreads load (for example merchant_id plus a hash of the key) and serve the back-office view another way. Add to the NFR-1 criterion that 45% of load comes from one merchant_id.
recommendation.expected_benefit: NFR-1 is shown under realistic merchant skew, and the Section 9.3 sizing is confirmed or corrected.
recommendation.issue: The hot-key capacity rests on an unverified partition ceiling and simple WCU arithmetic.
recommendation.rationale: If M-0001's partition throttles, idempotency checks fail for the merchant carrying 45% of peak traffic, which hits NFR-1 and NFR-2.
recommendation.verification: Load test of 900 TPS on one merchant_id for four hours with no DynamoDB throttling and p99 for the idempotency step ≤ 12 ms.

findings.statement: Section 9.3 relies on a per-partition ceiling of 10,000 WCU/s and counts each request as one write unit per operation. Items hold a serialised response of up to 4 KB, which may use more than one unit per write, and the LSI may also add write cost. The partition limit and the WCU sizing are not supported in the document and must be checked against DynamoDB documentation. The NFR-1 load test does not specify the 45% single-merchant skew, so it may never exercise the hot partition key.
findings.title: Hot-merchant DynamoDB capacity claim and the NFR-1 load profile need verification

At an 88% approval rate, 2 percentage points and a 2% relative change differ by about 0.24 points. With both a weighted score and a pairwise rule in play, the 'expected choice' in the FR-8 test is not uniquely defined.

recommendation.change_summary: State the unit in FR-8, Section 10.3 and the Section 24 routing row (for example '2.0 percentage points of approval_prior'). Specify the order of operations: compute the weighted score, then apply the FR-8 guard as an override, or the reverse. Add FR-8 boundary test cases at tolerance ±0.1.
recommendation.expected_benefit: FR-8 can be implemented and tested without guesswork.
recommendation.issue: FR-8 has no stated unit and two routing mechanisms that may disagree.
recommendation.rationale: Routing cost and approval rate are central business objectives, and the test needs one defined rule.
recommendation.verification: FR-8 boundary tests pass with the documented unit and order of operations.

findings.statement: FR-8 says 'more than 2%' and Section 10.3 says 'tolerance (default 2)', without stating whether this is 2 percentage points or a 2% relative change. Section 10.2 ranks acquirers by a weighted score, while Section 10.3 compares the cheapest acquirer with the highest-approval one, and a weekly review checks realised rates against a control slice. It is unclear which of these enforces the per-transaction FR-8. The FR-8 acceptance test only checks that the 'expected choice' is picked, so it cannot settle these readings.
findings.title: FR-8's 2% tolerance has no unit and the routing mechanisms conflict

FR-15 needs customer bank details, which are personal data and a payment destination, but no section defines how they are captured, verified or stored. The acceptance test cannot catch a wrong destination.

recommendation.change_summary: Add a subsection to Section 16.3 or 18 that defines: the API field or hosted form for the customer's account, name or account validation where the rail supports it, encrypted storage and retention, the refund_clearing ledger flow, and failure handling (returned payouts). List which Section 4 methods use this path. Extend the FR-15 acceptance test to cover validation failure and returned-payout cases.
recommendation.expected_benefit: FR-15 refunds go to the right account and are handled in line with NFR-7.
recommendation.issue: Refunds via customer bank payout are under-specified.
recommendation.rationale: FR-15 moves money to a destination that is not otherwise held in the system, and that destination is personal data under NFR-7.
recommendation.verification: FR-15 test covers a payout refund rejected for an invalid account and a returned payout reversing the refund_clearing posting.

findings.statement: FR-15 pays refunds as bank transfers to the customer's nominated account when a method has no refund API. Nothing in the document says how that account is collected, by the merchant or the customer, or how it is validated, stored or encrypted, or kept under NFR-7. The Section 6 payout account is the merchant's only, and Section 19 has no field for it. The FR-15 test only checks that a payout instruction is produced, so a mistaken or fraudulent destination would not be detected.
findings.title: Refunds paid to a customer's bank account have no data capture, verification or privacy design

findings.no_change_rationale: The ledger meets FR-10, P1 and P5 through atomic commit, immutability enforced at the database role level, and an invariant that is checked continuously, and its acceptance test can demonstrate this.
findings.statement: Journals are committed in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the state change and the outbox row. UPDATE and DELETE are revoked on journal and posting. The per-currency balance invariant is enforced at commit and recomputed every night. The worked journals in Section 14.2 balance. Together these meet FR-10, P1 and P5, and the FR-10 acceptance test (1 M-payment simulation, projection equal to recomputation) can actually demonstrate the requirement.
findings.title: Ledger design is consistent and verifiable

doc_anchors.quote: No floating-point type is used for amounts in any service, schema, or API payload.

sound_areas.why_sound: Amounts are integer minor units with ISO 4217 codes, and adapters reject any amount that would need rounding. This is consistent across P4, Section 15 and the BIGINT schema columns, so money values cannot be represented inconsistently.

doc_anchors.quote: up to 72 hours from first attempt (12 attempts including the first).

sound_areas.why_sound: The webhook retry schedule adds up to 12 attempts within 72 hours under either reading of the intervals, and the dead-letter store, replay and 30-day retention line up with Section 19.1 and the FR-12 acceptance test.

doc_anchors.quote: One merchant at 3× its rate limit does not move other merchants' p99 by more than 5%.

sound_areas.why_sound: Every FR and NFR in Section 2 has a named validation method and a pass/fail criterion. Most are concrete and measurable (for example NFR-9 noisy-neighbour at 3× the limit with ≤5% p99 shift), which gives the build a usable test baseline. The exceptions are covered in FND-004, FND-013 and FND-014.
